title: Question 5
stem:
Red light of wavelength $640\text{ nm}$ is incident normally on a diffraction grating having a line spacing of $1.7 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}$, as shown in Fig. 5.1.

{{figure:figure_5_1}}

Fig. 5.1 (not to scale)

The second order diffraction maximum of the light is at an angle $\theta$ to the direction of the incident light.

parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what has to be true for a bright maximum to form behind the grating - how does the extra distance travelled by light from one slit compared to the next relate to the wavelength?
Hint 2: Pick out your numbers carefully in SI units. The line spacing $d = 1.7 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}$, the wavelength needs converting from nm to m, and for this beam the order $n = 2$.
Hint 3: Rearrange to get $\sin\theta$ on its own, calculate its value, then use inverse sine to find $\theta$ and round to show it is about $49^{\circ}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall the grating rule for a bright spot**
Light from each slit spreads out by diffraction and then overlaps. You get a bright maximum where waves from neighbouring slits arrive in step, so the path difference must be a whole number of wavelengths. For normal incidence that condition is $$d\sin\theta = n\lambda$$ where $d$ is the slit spacing, $\theta$ is the angle to the straight-through direction, $n$ is the order number 0, 1, 2..., and $\lambda$ is the wavelength.

Step 2: **Put everything into metres and identify the order**
Here you are looking at the second order, so $n = 2$. $$\lambda = 640 \text{ nm} = 640 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m} = 6.40 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$$ $$d = 1.7 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}$$ Rearranged for the angle: $$\sin\theta = \frac{n\lambda}{d}$$

Step 3: **Calculate and show the angle**
Substitute the numbers: $$\sin\theta = \frac{2 \times 6.40 \times 10^{-7}}{1.7 \times 10^{-6}} = \frac{1.28 \times 10^{-6}}{1.7 \times 10^{-6}} = 0.753$$ Then: $$\theta = \sin^{-1}(0.753) = 48.8^{\circ}$$ This is $49^{\circ}$ to two significant figures, as required. A common slip is to leave the wavelength in nm, so always convert to m first to match $d$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Determine a different wavelength of visible light that will also produce a diffraction maximum at an angle of $49^{\circ}$.
hints: Hint 1: The grating and the angle have not changed, so the quantity $d\sin\theta$ is fixed. A different colour can give the same angle if it uses a different order number $n$.
Hint 2: Try the neighbouring orders $n = 1$ and $n = 3$ with $\lambda = d\sin49^{\circ} / n$ and keep the one that falls in the visible range of about $400 \text{ nm}$ to $700 \text{ nm}$.
parts.proper_answer: $d\sin\theta = 1.7 \times 10^{-6} \times \sin49^{\circ} = 1.28 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}$. For $n=3$, $\lambda = d\sin\theta / 3 = 4.3 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$, which is visible light.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use the same path difference with a new order**
At $49^{\circ}$ the path difference between adjacent slits is fixed: $$d\sin\theta = 1.7 \times 10^{-6} \times \sin49^{\circ}$$ $$d\sin\theta = 1.7 \times 10^{-6} \times 0.755 = 1.28 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}$$ Any wavelength that fits a whole number of times into this path difference will also give a maximum there: $$\lambda = \frac{d\sin\theta}{n}$$

Step 2: **Test other orders for visible light**
For $n = 2$ you get back the original $640 \text{ nm}$ red light. Try $n = 1$: $$\lambda = 1.28 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}$$ which is in the infra-red, not visible. Try $n = 3$: $$\lambda = \frac{1.28 \times 10^{-6}}{3} = 4.3 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$$ This is about $430 \text{ nm}$, which is violet-blue visible light, so it is a valid different wavelength. Higher orders give even shorter, non-visible wavelengths.
